segments.text: Constitutional structures explain where executive and legislative authority is located and how state institutions check one another.

In a parliamentary system the executive is politically linked to and accountable to the legislature. In a presidential system the executive is separately elected or separately constituted and enjoys a more distinct tenure. Separation of powers distributes state functions while checks and balances prevent concentration.

The basic difference lies in the relationship between executive and legislature. In a parliamentary model, the political executive ordinarily emerges from the legislature and remains responsible to it through mechanisms such as confidence. In a presidential model, the chief executive and legislature possess separate electoral or constitutional mandates and fixed or independently protected tenures.

This difference affects cabinet formation, removal, dissolution, legislative bargaining and the management of political deadlock. It does not mean that one system has checks and the other does not; rather, the checks operate through different institutional relationships.

blocks.text: Separation of powers and checks and balances

segments.text: Separation of powers is best understood as a principle against excessive concentration of governmental functions. Modern constitutions rarely place all legislative, executive and judicial activity in completely isolated compartments. Instead, they distribute primary functions while allowing controlled interaction.

Checks and balances are the institutional mechanisms that make that interaction accountable. Examples include legislative scrutiny of the executive, executive assent or veto mechanisms where constitutionally provided, judicial review, budgetary control, confirmation processes and constitutionally defined removal procedures. Their legitimacy depends on the constitutional allocation of power, not simply on whether they appear politically useful.

A strong comparative answer asks the same questions of each system: How is the head of government selected? Is executive tenure dependent on legislative confidence? Can the legislature be dissolved, and by whom? How are ministers appointed? What happens during institutional deadlock? How is judicial review organized? Using identical criteria prevents a comparison from becoming a list of unrelated national facts.

items.text: A parliamentary system links executive survival to legislative confidence. The head of government normally emerges from the parliamentary majority and remains politically accountable to the legislature.

A presidential system creates a more separate executive mandate and tenure. The executive and legislature derive authority separately, so conflict can occur without automatically removing either branch.

Separation of powers is not usually absolute. Modern constitutions distribute functions while creating checks: vetoes, confirmations, judicial review, legislative oversight, financial control and impeachment or removal procedures.
When comparing systems, use the same questions:
Who chooses the executive? Can the legislature remove it politically? Can the executive dissolve the legislature? How are ministers selected? How are institutional deadlocks managed?

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not write that parliamentary systems have no separation of powers. They have a fusion of executive-legislative leadership, but legal and institutional checks still exist.
